messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 23
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Vignette:
Aisha was 23 when she first began to speak about the night that had split her life into before and after. She had been driving home after dinner with her husband in the passenger seat when she turned through a familiar intersection and, in a moment she still replayed with humiliating clarity, struck a pedestrian crossing in front of them. The man survived, but not without serious injury, and what stayed with Aisha was not only the sound and confusion of the impact, but the immediate knowledge that she had been the one at the wheel. In the weeks that followed, she found herself returning again and again to the same sequence of seconds, asking how it could have been avoided if she had been more careful, more attentive, more anything. She would lie awake mentally reconstructing the route, the light changes, the speed of the car, the timing of her own glance, dwelling on every point at which the outcome might have been different. Even when she tried to stop, the thoughts came back with a force that made her feel cornered by her own mind.

Aisha had always been someone who organized her life carefully, and after the accident that need for control sharpened into a rigid effort not to think about what had happened. She tried to push the event out of her head whenever it surfaced, cutting herself off from conversations that might lead in that direction and forcing her attention onto work tasks or household routines. Yet the harder she tried to suppress the memory, the more intrusively it seemed to appear in fragments: the shape of a body on the road, the look on bystanders’ faces, the sickening awareness that ordinary movement could become disastrous in a single instant. These flashes were not abstract to her; they arrived as vivid reminders of the injured man and, later, of anyone who resembled him. Aisha noticed, with a jolt of dread, that people who looked similar to the victim—similar age, build, or features—could make her stomach tighten and her attention lock onto them before she could stop herself. On the street, in a grocery store, or passing someone in her apartment building, she would glance and then quickly look away, ashamed at how easily her mind seemed to attach the memory to an ordinary stranger.

Driving became the most obvious boundary in her life. At first she avoided getting behind the wheel altogether, then began refusing rides as a passenger as well, feeling trapped by the idea of being enclosed in a moving vehicle where anything could happen and where the memory felt close enough to touch. This avoidance shaped her days in practical ways. As a UX designer, Aisha had once commuted without much thought to client meetings and office days, but she increasingly structured her work around not having to travel. She preferred remote meetings and became anxious whenever an in-person obligation required her to consider transportation. The workplace itself, however, also became an unexpectedly sharp trigger. Her office was a modern open-plan environment with glass walls, polished floors, and a busy flow of colleagues arriving and leaving; something about simply being there could bring the accident back to her with force. Seeing coworkers gathered near the entrance, hearing the sound of footsteps in the lobby, or having to think about going home after a long day could suddenly make her feel as if she were back in that charged moment of movement and consequence. She would then become quiet and tense, trying to keep her face neutral while privately scanning for any reminder that might pull her back into the memory.

Over time, these patterns narrowed her world. She depended more on her husband for transportation and began arranging her life around routes, schedules, and contingencies that would keep her out of cars. Socially, she became more cautious when plans involved driving or when others spoke casually about traffic, accidents, or near misses. What finally brought her to seek help was not a single crisis but the accumulation of this small, exhausting narrowing of life and the fear that it would never ease. Aisha had come to feel that she could no longer trust her own mind to leave the event in the past; instead, it kept returning her to the scene, to the victim, to the possibility of similar faces in the crowd, and to the roads she no longer felt able to use. She was seeking help now because she wanted to understand why the memory remained so vivid and why everyday places like her office, or the sight of a man who resembled the person she had injured, could still jolt her into the same wave of dread. More than anything, she hoped to stop living as though one terrible mistake had permanently claimed the rest of her life.
